The agent warned him to pick a different one but could not confirm he did — security should verify the account is not using Winter2026! and force a reset if so (follow-up: today).

Caller behavior was odd: he repeatedly replied 'Okay, I'll try that' out of context and never described the 'separate issue' he called about. When the caller gives an off-topic reply, don't paper over it with 'Sounds good' and re-ask the same question. Name the mismatch and give concrete options, e.g. 'I didn't catch what the issue is — would you like the password reset steps, or should I have a technician call you back?'

Follow through on an offered walkthrough before pivoting to escalation. The agent said 'I can walk you through those steps next' but never delivered any steps; if the caller disengages, check whether they still want the walkthrough before logging a callback.

flags: Device LT-1006 (HP EliteBook 840) is running Windows 10 22H2, out of security support since 2025-10-14 — upgrade per KB0090 is still outstanding and should be treated as a security risk, not just a performance issue.
coaching: When the KB escalation condition is met (still slow after a restart), escalate immediately instead of repeating the same steps — the caller had to say 'still slow' and 'It's been like this for days' twice before the handover was offered.
When telling a caller their OS is no longer supported, always pair it with the concrete fix: recommend the KB0090 upgrade path to the caller directly, not just as a note for the technician.
Don't ask triage questions you won't act on — 'Once it finally starts, can you get your work done?' was never answered or used, which added friction to a short call.

strengths: Warm and empathetic throughout: 'I'm sorry it's still dragging, Kwame' and 'I hear you, Kwame, and this has gone on too long' acknowledged the caller's frustration by name.
Efficient start: confirmed identity, then asked about the existing ticket ('Are you calling about your existing ticket, I N C 1 0 0 0 5') instead of making the caller re-explain everything.

Clean handover: asked consent before escalating, confirmed the note was added, and set expectations clearly ('a technician will follow up with you') before a polite close. Numbers and the date were spoken in a natural, speakable way.
issues: Troubleshooting loop: after the caller said 'I restarted it, still slow,' the agent repeated essentially the same instruction ('please close any browser tabs and apps you aren't using, then restart'), so the caller had to say 'still slow' and 'It's been like this for days' twice before the agent escalated — the KB said to escalate once a restart hadn't helped.
The question 'Once it finally starts, can you get your work done?' was never answered or used, making it feel like an extra question that went nowhere.

Telling the caller their Windows version 'is no longer supported' without offering a concrete next step for that (e.g., an upgrade) risked worrying them; it was only mentioned as something the technician would see.
experience.summary: A warm, efficient call with a clean escalation, slightly marred by a repetitive troubleshooting loop that made the caller repeat themselves before the agent handed over.

issues: Over-promised and under-delivered: the agent asked 'Would you like me to go over what you should bring with you?', Priya said yes, and then the agent admitted 'I don't have a specific list of what to bring, so please check with them on arrival' — a wasted turn that leaves the caller with nothing after agreeing.

The first failure message was ambiguous about what to do next ('Please try again in a little while, and I'll send the code as soon as the texts are working again'), which seems to have confused Priya into replying 'Okay, done. It's still not working' as if she had completed a step.

The closing line repeated the failure explanation already given twice ('Texts aren't going through right now, so I couldn't verify you or move your sign-in approvals'), adding length without new information.
experience.summary: A calm, kind, and safe call that clearly explained the SMS outage and gave a workable in-person alternative, but it lost polish by offering a 'what to bring' list it couldn't provide and by slightly confusing the caller about what to do next.

coaching: Give one troubleshooting action per turn: the opening step combined 'click the arrow next to the microphone icon' with 'tell me whether the right microphone is selected,' which produced the confused reply 'Yes, please.'
When a caller answers with bare 'Okay' twice in a row, stop re-asking the same question — simplify the step or offer to log a ticket sooner, rather than on the third attempt.
If a caller says 'I'll hold,' explicitly correct the expectation: there is no hold or live transfer on this line, so confirm the ticket is logged and a technician will call back.

strengths: Warm, calm tone throughout: greeted Yuki by name, and when the caller struggled, said kindly 'It sounds like that step may be getting in the way, and that's fine' before offering a ticket instead of pushing more steps.

Honest and plain-spoken about the status check: 'I couldn't reach the Zoom status page, so I can't confirm whether it's a wider problem, but let's keep going on your end.' No jargon, no tool mentions.

Clean handover: read the ticket summary back for confirmation before logging, gave the number slowly and speakably ('I N C 1 0 0 2 2'), and set expectations clearly: 'A technician will follow up with you, and nothing else is needed from you right now.'
issues: The first troubleshooting step packed two things into one turn ('click the small arrow next to the microphone icon... Tell me whether the right microphone is selected'), which likely contributed to the caller's confused non-answer 'Yes, please.'

The agent then re-asked essentially the same question three times in a row ('Which microphone does Zoom show as selected?' then 'Are you seeing that menu on your screen right now?') while the caller only replied 'Okay' — it adapted gracefully on the third try, but could have simplified or offered the ticket sooner.
When the caller said 'Okay, I'll hold,' the agent didn't acknowledge that there would be no hold or transfer, which could leave the caller briefly unsure what was happening next.
experience.summary: A kind, clear call where the agent gracefully pivoted to logging a ticket when the caller couldn't follow the troubleshooting steps, though the compound first instruction and repeated questioning caused some early confusion.
